content: Write a cover letter for an operations manager job at a logistics company.

# Cover Letter — Operations Manager

**[Your Name]**
[City, State] | [Phone] | [Email] | [LinkedIn]

[Date]

[Hiring Manager Name]
[Company Name]
[Company Address]

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I'm writing to apply for the Operations Manager position at [Company Name]. With [X] years of experience managing high-volume distribution and transportation operations, I've built a track record of improving throughput and on-time performance while controlling cost per shipment — and I'm eager to bring that focus to a company known for [specific detail: e.g., its cold-chain capabilities, regional LTL network, or recent expansion into the Southeast].

In my current role as [Your Title] at [Current Company], I oversee daily operations for a [size] sq. ft. facility processing [volume] orders per day with a team of [#] associates across [#] shifts. Highlights include:

- **Improved on-time, in-full (OTIF) delivery from [X]% to [Y]%** by redesigning wave planning and rebalancing dock schedules, which also cut trailer dwell time by [X] hours.
- **Reduced operating cost per unit by [X]%** ([$ amount] annually) through labor-standard revisions, slotting optimization, and renegotiating rates with [#] regional carriers.
- **Cut recordable safety incidents by [X]%** in [timeframe] by launching a daily gemba walk and near-miss reporting program, moving the site to [X] days without a lost-time injury.
- **Led the implementation of [WMS/TMS system]**, delivering the cutover on schedule with less than [X] days of productivity disruption.

Beyond the metrics, I'd describe my management style as visible and data-driven. I spend most of my day on the floor, I run tiered daily huddles so problems surface within hours instead of weeks, and I invest heavily in developing supervisors — [#] of my direct reports have been promoted into leadership roles. I hold a [degree/certification, e.g., Lean Six Sigma Green Belt] and am comfortable owning P&L, capacity planning, and cross-functional escalations with sales and customer service.

I'm particularly interested in [Company Name] because [specific, genuine reason — a growth initiative, service model, or value that connects to your experience]. I'd welcome the chance to discuss how I can help your team hit its [service/cost/growth] targets.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

---

**Tips for customizing this:**
- Replace every bracket — hiring managers spot generic letters instantly. Numbers are what make this letter work, so dig up real ones even if they're estimates you can defend.
- Mirror 2–3 keywords from the job posting (e.g., "3PL," "yard management," "DOT compliance," "SLA adherence").
- Keep it to one page. If you're over ~400 words, cut the weakest bullet.
- If you're changing industries, add one sentence early on connecting your background to logistics-specific challenges.

Want me to tailor this to a specific job posting or your actual resume? Paste either one and I'll revise it.
I want to see this written for a different reader than the first version. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

# Cover Letter — Operations Manager (for a reader who already knows you)

*Assumption: this version is for an internal promotion, a role you've been referred into, or a hiring manager you've already spoken with. Since they know your track record, the letter skips the résumé recap and spends its space on what you'd actually do in the seat.*

---

**[Your Name]**
[Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

Dear [Name],

Thanks for encouraging me to put this in writing — I'd like to be considered for the Operations Manager role at [site/region].

You already know the numbers from [current site/role], so I'll skip the recap and go to what I think the job actually requires right now.

From what I've seen, [site/region] has three live constraints: [constraint 1, e.g., inbound dock congestion that's pushing OTIF into the low 90s], [constraint 2, e.g., a supervisor bench that's one resignation away from being thin], and [constraint 3, e.g., cost per unit drifting up as volume mix shifts toward smaller, more frequent orders]. My read is that the first two are the same problem — the schedule can't flex because there aren't enough people who can run a shift independently.

Here's how I'd approach the first 90 days:

- **Days 1–30:** Work the floor across all shifts before changing anything. Validate the labor standards against what's actually happening, and get a real picture of which supervisors are ready for more.
- **Days 30–60:** Fix dock scheduling and appointment discipline first — it's the cheapest lever and it makes every downstream metric easier to read. Start a structured development track for [#] high-potential leads.
- **Days 60–90:** Bring a costed plan for [larger initiative — slotting rework, carrier rebid, automation pilot] with a defensible payback period, rather than asking for headcount.

What I'd want from you: clarity on how much latitude I have on [carrier mix / capex / staffing model], and a straight answer on whether [known constraint — a customer commitment, a system migration, a pending lease decision] is fixed or negotiable. That changes the sequencing significantly.

I've been ready for a P&L of this size for a while, and I'd rather grow into it here than somewhere I'd have to learn the network from scratch. Happy to talk through any of the above whenever it's useful.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

**What changed and why:**

| First version | This version |
|---|---|
| Established credibility with metrics | Assumes credibility; spends space on diagnosis |
| Described past achievements | Proposes a forward plan |
| Formal, arms-length tone | Direct, collegial, asks something back |
| ~400 words | ~300 words |

**Two cautions:** First, only make claims about the site's problems that you can actually support — a confident misdiagnosis is worse than a generic letter. Second, if a formal HR process is involved, this letter may be read by people who *don't* know you, so ask whether it goes to the hiring manager directly or into a system. If it's the latter, use the first version and send this one as a follow-up note.
I need a shorter version of this for a different placement. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

# Short Version — Operations Manager (~150 words, main point first)

*Best for: email body, internal note, or a message where the letter sits alongside a résumé that carries the detail.*

---

Subject: Operations Manager — [site/region]

Dear [Name],

I'd like to be considered for the Operations Manager role at [site/region]. You know my numbers, so here's my read on the job instead.

[Site/region]'s dock congestion and thin supervisor bench are the same problem: the schedule can't flex because too few people can run a shift alone. Fix the bench and OTIF follows.

My first 90 days: work all shifts before changing anything, then tighten appointment discipline — cheapest lever, and it makes every other metric readable. By day 90, bring you a costed plan for [initiative] with a real payback, not a headcount request.

One thing I'd need from you: whether [known constraint] is fixed or negotiable. That changes the sequencing.

Ready for a P&L this size, and I'd rather grow into it here than learn a new network from scratch.

Best,
[Your Name]

---

**What I cut:** the three-part constraint list (kept the strongest one), the day-by-day phase breakdown, and the latitude question on carrier mix/capex — those are better raised in conversation.

**Note on placement:** if this goes out as an email, the first line is doing the work of a subject line and an opener at once. Make sure the résumé or attachment carries the metrics this version now assumes.
We can't include a claim about results in this one, for reasons on our end. Take out the claim about results and leave everything else as it is.

---

**What I removed:** "Fix the bench and OTIF follows." — the one sentence promising a specific performance outcome. Everything else is unchanged.

**Two phrases to check, in case your constraint is broader than I read it:**
- "cheapest lever, and it makes every other metric readable" — implies an outcome, though it's framed as reasoning rather than a promise.
- "with a real payback" — refers to a future plan's projected return, not a result you've delivered.

If either needs to go, say so and I'll cut them without touching anything else.
